title: MAHIPAL SINGH ALIAS MANOHAR SINGH versus NATIONAL HIGHWAYS AUTHORITY OF INDIA

paras.text:
HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Appeal From Order No. 80 of 2025
Mahipal Singh @ Manohar Singh and others
........Appellants

Versus
National Highways Authority of India and another
......Respondents
Present:-
Mr. Rajesh Pandey, Advocate for the appellants.
Mr. Raunak Pant, Advocate for the respondent no. 1.
Mr. V.D. Bisen, Addl. CSC for the State.
Hon'ble Ravindra Maithani, J. (Oral)
The challenge in this appeal is made to the judgment and
order dated 10.02.2025 passed in Misc. Civil Case (Arbitration) No. 99
of 2021, National Highways Authority of India v. Mahipal Singh @
Manohar Singh and others under Section 34 of the Arbitration and
Conciliation Act, 1996 ("the AC Act, 1996"), by the court of the District
Judge, Udham Singh Nagar. By it, while setting aside the arbitral
award dated 05.02.2021, the matter was remanded to the
Arbitrator/Collector for providing opportunity of hearing to the parties
and to dispose of it in accordance with law in the light of the directions
made in the impugned judgment and order.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties and perused
the record.
3. Learned counsel for the appellants submits that under
Section 34 of the AC Act, 1996 while setting aside an award, the
matter cannot be remanded; it is not a scheme of the AC Act, 1996. He
would submit that the only permissible mode for remand of the matter
is under Section 34(4) of the AC Act, 1996 under which, there should
be a written request from a party, so as to give the arbitral tribunal an

2
opportunity to resume the arbitral proceedings or to take such other
action as in the opinion of arbitral tribunal will eliminate the grounds
for setting aside the arbitral award. It is argued that beyond it, in a
proceeding under Section 34 of the AC Act, 1996 the order of remand
cannot be passed. He would also submit that the remand has been
made in a routine manner in order to appreciate the law point, which
could have been done in a proceeding under Section 34 of the AC Act,
1996 itself.
4. In support of his contentions, learned counsel for the
appellants has placed reliance on the principle of law as laid down by
the Bombay High Court in the case of Jyoti Construction Company v.
Municipal Corporation of the City of Thane (Arbitration Appeal No. 13
of 2020).
5. In the case of Jyoti Construction Company (supra), the
Hon'ble Bombay High Court has, in fact, relied upon the principle of
law as laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Kinnari
Mullick and another v. Ghanshyam Das Damani, (2018) 11 SCC 328,
with regard to remand under the provisions of the AC Act, 1996. In
para 15 of the judgment in the case of Kinnari Mullick (supra), the
Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed as follows:-
"15. On a bare reading of this provision, it is amply
clear that the Court can defer the hearing of the
application filed under Section 34 for setting aside the
award on a written request made by a party to the
arbitration proceedings to facilitate the Arbitral Tribunal by
resuming the arbitral proceedings or to take such other
action as in the opinion of the Arbitral Tribunal will
eliminate the grounds for setting aside the arbitral award.
The quintessence for exercising power under this
provision is that the arbitral award has not been set

3
aside. Further, the challenge to the said award has been
set up under Section 34 about the deficiencies in the
arbitral award which may be curable by allowing the
Arbitral Tribunal to take such measures which can
eliminate the grounds for setting aside the arbitral award.
No power has been invested by Parliament in the Court
to remand the matter to the Arbitral Tribunal except to
adjourn the proceedings for the limited purpose
mentioned in sub-section (4) of Section 34. This legal
position has been expounded in McDermott International
Inc. [McDermott International Inc. v. Burn Standard Co. Ltd.,
(2006) 11 SCC 181] In para 8 of the said decision, the
Court observed thus: (Bhaskar Industrial case [Bhaskar
Industrial Development Ltd. v. South Western Railway, 2016
SCC OnLine Kar 8330] , SCC OnLine Kar)
"8. ... Parliament has not conferred any power of
remand to the Court to remit the matter to the Arbitral
Tribunal except to adjourn the proceedings as provided
under sub-section (4) of Section 34 of the Act. The object
of sub-section (4) of Section 34 of the Act is to give an
opportunity to the Arbitral Tribunal to resume the
arbitral proceedings or to enable it to take such other
action which will eliminate the grounds for setting
aside the arbitral award."
(emphasis supplied)
6. However, in para 16 of the judgment in the case of
Kinnari Mullick (supra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court observed that "the
limited discretion available to the Court under Section 34(4) can
be exercised only upon a written application made in that behalf
by a party to the arbitration proceedings."
7. On the other hand, learned counsel for the respondent
no. 1 submits that in a proceeding under Section 34 of the AC Act,
1996 the matter can be remanded. He would refer to the principle of
law as laid down in the case of National Highways Authority of India v.
P. Nagaraju alias Cheluvaiah and another, (2022) 15 SCC 1, wherein
in para 47, the Hon'ble Supreme Court relied on the law laid down by

4
the Hon'ble Supreme Court on this aspect in the case of Project
Director, National Highways No. 45 E and 220 National Highways
Authority of India v. M. Hakeem and another, (2021) 9 SCC 1.
8. In the case of M. Hakeem (supra), the Hon'ble Supreme
Court in para 42, observed as follows:-
"42. It can therefore be said that this question has now
been settled finally by at least 3 decisions [McDermott
International Inc. v. Burn Standard Co. Ltd., (2006) 11
SCC 181] , [Kinnari Mullick v. Ghanshyam Das Damani,
(2018) 11 SCC 328 : (2018) 5 SCC (Civ) 106] , [Dakshin
Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Navigant Technologies
(P) Ltd., (2021) 7 SCC 657] of this Court. Even otherwise,
to state that the judicial trend appears to favour an
interpretation that would read into Section 34 a power to
modify, revise or vary the award would be to ignore the
previous law contained in the 1940 Act; as also to ignore
the fact that the 1996 Act was enacted based on
the Uncitral Model Law on International Commercial
Arbitration, 1985 which, as has been pointed out
in Redfern and Hunter on International Arbitration, makes
it clear that, given the limited judicial interference on
extremely limited grounds not dealing with the merits of an
award, the "limited remedy" under Section 34 is
coterminous with the "limited right", namely, either to set
aside an award or remand the matter under the
circumstances mentioned in Section 34 of the
Arbitration Act, 1996."
(emphasis supplied)
9. Learned counsel for the respondent no. 1 also submits
that if the award is not in accordance with law, in such circumstance
also, in a proceeding under Section 34 of the AC Act, 1996 the award
may be set aside and remanded to the arbitrator.

5
10. Before proceeding further, it would be apt to reproduce
sub-section (4) of Section 34 of the AC Act, 1996 which reads as
under:-
"34. Application for setting aside arbitral award.-(1)
Recourse to a Court against an arbitral award may be made only by
an application for setting aside such award in accordance with sub-section (2) and sub-section (3).
..............................................................................................
..............................................................................................
(4) On receipt of an application under sub-section (1), the
Court may, where it is appropriate and it is so requested by a party,
adjourn the proceedings for a period of time determined by it in
order to give the arbitral tribunal an opportunity to resume the
arbitral proceedings or to take such other action as in the opinion of
arbitral tribunal will eliminate the grounds for setting aside the
arbitral award.
..............................................................................................
............................................................................................"
11. In the case of M. Hakeem (supra), in para 42, as quoted
hereinabove, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that in a proceeding
under Section 34 of the AC Act, 1996 the award may either be set
aside or remanded under the circumstances mentioned in Section 34
of the AC Act, 1996. This is what has been referred to by the Hon'ble
Supreme Court in the case of P. Nagaraju (supra).
12. At the cost of repetition, it is noted that in the case of
Kinnari Mullick (supra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court has categorically
held that the limited discretion available to the Court under Section
34(4) can be exercised only upon a written application made in that
behalf by a party to the arbitration proceedings. In fact, the purport of
Section 34(4) of the AC Act, 1996 is to give an opportunity to the
arbitral tribunal to resume the arbitral proceedings or to take such

6
other action as in the opinion of arbitral tribunal will eliminate the
grounds for setting aside the arbitral award.
13. The scheme of sub-section (4) of Section 34 of the AC Act,
1996 provides that on an application of a party, in appropriate cases,
the proceedings under Section 34 of the AC Act, 1996 may be
adjourned for a period of time so as to give the arbitral tribunal an
opportunity to resume the arbitral proceedings or to take such other
action as in the opinion of arbitral tribunal will eliminate the grounds
for setting aside the arbitral award. Under this scheme, the award is
not set aside. The proceedings under Section 34 of the AC Act, 1996
are merely adjourned for future date so that in between the arbitral
tribunal may resume the proceedings or to take such other action so
as to eliminate the grounds for setting aside the arbitral award. In the
instant case, it has not been done. By the impugned judgment and
order, the award has been set aside and the matter was remanded for
decision afresh. This may not be done under sub-section (4) of Section
34 of the AC Act, 1996.
14. Also, in view of the settled law, before exercising
discretion under Section 34(4) of the AC Act, 1996, there should be an
application filed by the party to the arbitration. In the instant case,
admittedly, no application was filed by any of the parties. The court
while exercising discretion observed that the arbitral award deserves to
be set aside with the direction to the arbitrator to decide the whole
controversy raised before him, afresh.
15. As such, such order is not stipulated under Section 34(4)
of the AC Act, 1996. Therefore, this Court is of the view that the

7
impugned judgment and order is not in accordance with law.
Accordingly, the impugned judgment and order deserves to be set
aside.
16. The appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and order
is set aside. The court concerned is requested to decide the application
under Section 34 of the AC Act, 1996 in accordance with law.
